chapter_theme: The end of the war of மண்மகள் இலம்பகம்: Ariccandan's rally fails, Civakan kills the usurper's sons and then Kattiyangaran, who meets his death speaking of karma and fate and vowing on his honour, and the Earth goddess passes to Civakan.

cast.role: the hero, son of Saccandan and Vijayai, called குமரன், காளை, சீவக சாமி here
the minister who seized Saccandan's throne, killed by Civakan in this run
a warrior on Kattiyangaran's side who rallies the routed men (named at 2299)
the army Kattiyangaran leads against Civakan
the sons of the king who ride out against Civakan and die
the Earth goddess (பூமி தேவி), figured as the bride Civakan wins

2302.reading: Ariccandan ends his rallying speech: men who die helping the leader who raised and kept them are garlanded with karpaka flowers and embrace the women of heaven, are crowned with poets' garlands of praise, and stand on the hero-stone with their valour shown and their fame spread wide.
2302.event: Ariccandan finishes urging the routed men back to the fight.

claims.claim: a warrior who dies helping the master who sustained him wins heaven's women, poets' praise and a hero-stone

2302.nuance: Three rewards are stacked, one in each world: heaven (கற்பக மாலை, அரமகளிர்), the poets' word, and the stone on earth. The speaker is named in 2299 (அரிச்சந்தன்); this verse names him only by என்றான், and the next verse shows the men he rallied going down before Civakan's arrows.

2303.reading: The men sharpen their weapons as one thrusts a spear into green bamboo, bind on belts and anklets, put gold into their mouths, roar to strike fear, and become the day's food for the arrows in the young prince's hand.
2303.event: Rallied, the enemy warriors arm and charge, and Civakan's arrows cut them down.
2303.nuance: Putting gold in the mouth (காஞ்சனத் தளிவம் வாய்க்கிட்டு) is the warrior's preparation for death; the speech of 2302 is answered at once by the slaughter.

2304.reading: As a cloud rising in the north sweeps rightward wreathed in lightning and pours thundering rain on the west, Civakan drove his chariot in a flash with gold-armoured shoulders, and the rain of arrows from his bow stood like a falling stream.
2304.event: Civakan drives into the enemy and pours arrows on them.

2305.reading: Severed heads lodged on the elephants' bodies, held up on the arrows driven through them as on stalks, looked like red lotuses on a terrace, and their red eyes like bees crowded to sip the pollen.
2305.nuance: A battlefield-as-garden figure; it prepares the fuller lotus-pond allegory of 2311.

2306.reading: As if the moon and all the hills shook and the great earth gave way, with conches wailing, elephants falling, horses rolling and gold banners snapping, the sons of the king appeared on their chariots roaring like lions.
2306.event: The usurper's sons ride out in their chariots against Civakan.
2306.nuance: அவன் சிறுவர் says only 'his sons'; that they are Kattiyangaran's is read from 2311, where the king's children are the stamens round the king.

2307.reading: As when the cool moon with its crowd of stars wrestles with the young sun of saffron rays, the sons' chariots tangled with the generous hero's in a flash like lightning in cloud, and the hot arrows from their bows crowded so thick that they hid the sun.
2307.event: The sons close with Civakan's chariot and their arrows darken the sky.

2308.reading: Like the white moon seized by a serpent, the hero, red with the blade's light, set the right-whorled conch to his mouth and blew; the earth's people trembled as at the roar of the east wind, his serpent-fierce bow bent, and the lord's eyes spat fire.
2308.event: Civakan blows his conch and draws his bow in anger.

2309.reading: As the Ganga rushes into the sea, the young bull's bow poured hot arrows till they filled the mouths of the youths who had roared, and pierced through the chest they lay dead on their chariots like lions in a long cave.
2309.event: Civakan's arrows kill the usurper's sons on their chariots.
2309.nuance: The last word, printed இஞ்சினார், is read as 'lay dead' only from the simile; the line is likely corrupt.

2310.reading: White umbrellas fell, kings rose to the far sky, hosts of ghouls danced, jackals feasted, headless trunks danced everywhere, elephants and horses toppled, and the red-eyed Civakasami's brows curved in wrath.
2310.event: The field fills with the dead as Civakan's anger mounts.
2310.nuance: Kings 'climbing the sky' (நீள்விசும்பு ஏற) is the battlefield death 2302 promised as heaven, now told of the enemy.

2311.reading: The battlefield is a lotus pond: the swords are the outer petals, the elephants the inner petals, the kings the stamens, the king's sons the inner ring, and the king himself the seed-pod; and having slowly fed on the flower in order, the holy bee flew up onto the pod.
2311.event: Having destroyed the army and the sons, Civakan turns on the king himself.
2311.nuance: The allegory turns the slaughter into a bee's orderly feeding from the outside in, so the order of the battle is also the order of a hierarchy, ending at its centre; the bee is called பவித்திரம், holy.

2312.reading: The king, whose mountainous chest is kissed by the pearls of women's breasts, saw it and burned with rage, and the noble one, whose strong shoulders the bow kisses, reddened like fire.
2312.event: Kattiyangaran and Civakan face each other in fury.
2312.nuance: The fourfold முத்தம் pun (pearl and kiss) sets the lover's chest of the king against the archer's shoulders of the hero.

2313.reading: Seated on the fierce elephant Asanivegam, at whose musk a wild tusker swallows its own must, fears and runs leaving its mate, the king of the flashing garland spoke to the hero.
2313.event: Kattiyangaran, mounted on his war elephant, addresses Civakan.

2314.reading: Kattiyangaran says that for those with good deeds poison drunk becomes nectar, and for those without, nectar becomes poison, such is the working of deeds; so the truly wise never think 'I can kill him' or 'he will kill me'.

claims.claim: by good deeds poison becomes nectar, and without them nectar becomes poison
the wise do not think of killing or being killed, since the outcome lies with deeds

2314.nuance: The usurper, about to die, gives the whole outcome to deeds and none to his own seizure of the throne. The story has given another cause: Dharmadattan warned at 245 that Fortune would turn from him if he seized the king. Here karma and the ruler's fault are both on the page, in different mouths.

2315.reading: He goes on: who can ruin those whose fortune is in their grasp, and can those of great fortune be made empty? the cool-rayed moon may scorch till men tremble, and the hostile sun may yield coolness.

claims.claim: no one can undo the fortune that is someone's lot, though it may reverse the natural order

2315.nuance: பொறி is fortune as allotted; the reversed moon and sun of lines 3-4 can be read as what fortune can do, or as his own fall. The end of line 4 (சந்து மாலியும்) is unclear as divided.

2316.reading: A lamp of pearl-strung gold stand does not flare up after its ghee and its wick are spent; its flame only dwindles; so when the two kinds of deed have worn away, who can keep wealth from perishing, however anxiously he guards it?

claims.claim: when one's twofold deeds are spent, wealth perishes and no care can keep it

2316.nuance: இருவினை, both good and bad deeds, makes the fuel of wealth all of one's karma, not only merit; the usurper reads his own lost throne as a lamp that has burnt out rather than one taken from its owner.

2317.reading: The hero, baring his jewel-like teeth, laughed so they flashed and said 'you are afraid'; the king answered that victory comes by fate, but if he blinked when a spear came, then the hero might say so and laugh, and bade him come at him.
2317.event: Civakan mocks Kattiyangaran's talk of fate as fear, and Kattiyangaran challenges him.

claims.claim: victory in battle comes by fate

2317.nuance: Civakan's mockery reads the fate speech of 2314 to 2316 as cowardice; the king separates the two, granting the outcome to fate while keeping courage, the unblinking eye, as his own.

2318.reading: With the bangled generous hand that had set right the anklets of soft-footed women, wiped the tears they wept when hurt and so been smeared with their collyrium, he seized the cruel bow and spoke roaring like thunder.
2318.event: Kattiyangaran takes up his bow and speaks.
2318.nuance: The hand is a lover's before it is a warrior's; the next verse's elephant shows it is the king's, and the image echoes 2312's lover's chest.

2319.reading: He vows that if he loses in valour he may become a base man of a heart that fears his wife and kills the face of the guest, and fuming he split through the press of bow and sword, glared, drove his killing elephant forward and fitted one last arrow.
2319.event: Kattiyangaran vows, charges on his elephant and sets an arrow to his bow.

claims.claim: a man who fears his wife and turns from his guest is base

2319.nuance: The self-curse names faults of the house, not the field: the worst he can imagine becoming is a henpecked man who shames a guest. The vow is in the first person (தோற்பின்), while the description around it is the narrator's.

2320.reading: Before he could draw and loose the arrow he had fitted, the hero of the sharp white spear and diamond ornaments shot with a bright crescent-headed arrow and cut the arrow, the bow and its string so that they fell.
2320.event: Civakan cuts Kattiyangaran's arrow, bow and bowstring with one crescent arrow.

2321.reading: Blazing that his arrow and bow were cut, he gripped his gold sword in fury and leapt at the hero's chariot crying 'let the gold-crowned one fall', like a god descending from the golden world.
2321.event: Disarmed, Kattiyangaran leaps sword in hand onto Civakan's chariot.

2322.reading: The red one's golden arrows went into the chest that had been a battlefield for the breasts of women, and with them his life went; eyes burning, lips bitten, he fell like the moon falling from the dark sky.
2322.event: Civakan's arrows pierce Kattiyangaran's chest and he falls dead.
2322.nuance: The lover's chest of 2312 and 2318 becomes the target; the moon-fall answers 2308 and 2324, where Civakan is the moon in the serpent's mouth and then the sun freed from it.

2323.reading: As if the Kali-rule called Kattiyangaran had perished, the warriors beat the drums proclaiming that the enmity was over and the work of arms should cease, and roared; and the Earth goddess, shedding tears of blood, gave her longing to him.
2323.event: With Kattiyangaran dead, Civakan's warriors proclaim the war's end.
2323.nuance: கலியரசு names the usurper's reign as the age of Kali, a rule against order rather than a single wrong. Line 4 (விட்டமு தவன்கண் ஆர்வம் மண்மகள் நீக்கினாள்) can be divided so that the Earth puts away her grief or turns her love to Civakan; the ilampakam's name rests on it.

2324.reading: Civakan was like the young sun that a serpent had seized in the forehead of the sea and held in its cheek while the world trembled, standing forth after many days when it had split open the jewelled serpent's mouth.
2324.nuance: The 'many days' (பல்பகல்) under the serpent are the years of the usurpation since his father's death; the victory is figured as release from an eclipse, not a conquest.

2325.reading: The warriors gathered like the hosts of stars round the moon, kings surrounded him, the city roared like the sea, its lamps thronged like stars; and hearing the victory garland proclaimed, the faultless Vijayai's eyes filled with tears and grew cool.
2325.event: The army and kings gather round Civakan, and Vijayai hears of his victory and weeps for joy.
2325.nuance: Vijayai's cooled eyes close the grief that began when she left the city on the peacock machine; கேடில் (faultless, without ruin) is said of her at the moment her ruin is reversed.

2326.reading: With the crowned kings' garlands and fire-edged swords as jewelled pots and their blood standing for the bathing water, he was bathed as for anointing, and came to enjoy as one the paired breasts of the Earth goddess of gold garlands and fine jewels.
2326.event: Civakan, as if anointed in the enemy's blood, takes the earth as his bride.
2326.nuance: The coronation bath (மண்ணுநீர்) is made of the battlefield, and the winning of the kingdom is told as a marriage, the hero's last bride after his eight wives: this is the ilampakam's மண்மகள்.

links.note: Kural 780 says a death that fills with tears the eyes of those who sustained one is worth begging for; Ariccandan's speech promises rewards to men who die helping the leader who raised and kept them (தற்புறந் தந்து வைத்த தலைமகற்கு).
links.teaches: Together they show the couplet's patron-bond being used as a battlefield appeal, and that it can be spent on a bad master: the leader these men are asked to die for is the usurper, and the speech wins only their deaths.

gains.a: Ariccandan's speech is seen to rest on the moral claim of the sustained man's debt, not merely on bribes of heaven
gains.b: the couplet's ideal is shown with its blind spot: it weighs the bond to the sustainer and not whether the sustainer deserves the death

links.note: The Purananuru poem says warriors who stand under arrows care nothing for fields because, dying, they wed flawless women in the high world; Ariccandan offers the same heavenly women (கடியரமகளிர்) and adds the poets' praise and the hero-stone.
links.teaches: The pairing shows the Sangam promise of heavenly brides surviving into the Jain epic as a commander's rallying formula, now stacked with fame and stone into a three-world reward, while the following verse turns its hearers into food for the hero's arrows.

gains.a: the speech is placed in a long tradition of the warrior's reward, which explains why the beaten men return to the fight
gains.b: the poem's confident claim is set in a story where those who believe it fight for the losing, unjust side

links.note: Dharmadattan warned Kattiyangaran that a king is a fire that turns nectar or poison as it will; at his end Kattiyangaran says it is good or bad deeds that turn poison to nectar and nectar to poison.
links.teaches: The same nectar-and-poison figure moves from the wronged king's power to impersonal karma, and the shift lets the usurper blame his fall on deeds in general rather than on the king he wronged, as he was warned.

links.note: Kural 380 holds nothing is stronger than fate, which forestalls any scheme; Kattiyangaran says the wise do not think of killing or being killed because deeds decide.
links.teaches: The epic gives the couplet's fatalism to a schemer whose own plot made the war, so the reader sees how the doctrine that fate outruns all devices can also serve to excuse the devices one has already used.

gains.a: the speech is seen to quote a sanctioned teaching, so its self-serving use is the point and not an error of doctrine
gains.b: the couplet gains a test case where fate is invoked by the guilty party at the moment of reckoning

links.note: The Naladiyar quatrain says that as darkness rushes back when the lamp's oil runs out, evil settles in when good deeds are spent; Kattiyangaran says that as a lamp dwindles when ghee and wick are gone, wealth perishes when the two kinds of deed wear away.
links.teaches: Both make karma the lamp's fuel, but the quatrain teaches renewing merit by austerity while the epic's usurper uses the image to explain the loss of a throne, so the lamp shows its political use: a fall can be read as fuel run out instead of a wrong repaid.

gains.a: the speech is seen to draw on a renunciant teaching image, sharpened by counting both good and bad deeds as fuel
gains.b: the quatrain's image is applied to kingship and wealth in a story, where it can be heard as self-excuse

links.note: Kural 775 counts it flight for the fierce to blink when a spear is thrown; Kattiyangaran says that if he blinks when a spear comes, Civakan may laugh.
links.teaches: The king splits outcome from courage: he grants victory to fate yet stakes his honour on the couplet's unblinking eye, so the pair shows the unblinking gaze as the one part of valour fate cannot take.

gains.a: the boast is read against a fixed measure of valour, which answers Civakan's taunt of fear
gains.b: the couplet's standard is shown held by a man who believes the battle's result is not his to decide

links.note: Kural 904 says the man who fears his wife gains no distinction from his deeds; Kattiyangaran's self-curse is that if he loses in valour he may become a base man who fears his wife (இல்லாளை அஞ்சி) and slights a guest.
links.teaches: The vow ranks fear of one's wife as a disgrace equal to defeat in battle, which shows the couplet's household fault serving as a warrior's measure of shame, the worst a king can wish on himself.

gains.a: the oath's odd household content is explained: it names a vice the moral tradition already marks as ruin of a man's action
gains.b: the couplet's fault is seen weighed against cowardice in war, which places it among the gravest failures of manhood

links.note: Boothappandiyan's vow wishes on himself, if he fails, separation from his wife, a weak sceptre and the loss of friends; Kattiyangaran's vow wishes on himself fear of his wife and the shame of slighting a guest.
links.teaches: Both are conditional self-curses whose penalties are drawn from household and court rather than the field, so the pair shows the vanjinam form keeping its structure into the epic while the epic gives it to the losing usurper, who dies at once.

gains.a: the speech is identified as a vanjinam of a known form, with its self-curse clauses
gains.b: the Sangam vow is seen in a story where it is not fulfilled, so the vow's force is shown as a matter of the speaker's cause

links.note: Dharmadattan warned that if Kattiyangaran seized the king who made him, Fortune would turn from him; here his rule, called a Kali-reign, perishes and the war is declared over.
links.teaches: The usurper's fall fulfils the councillor's warning given before the crime, so the story names his own deed as cause even though, dying, he gave everything to karma at 2314 to 2316.

links.note: Vijayai asked that her son be told all the evil she suffered after her lord died and be brought to her; here hearing his victory her tear-filled eyes grow cool.
links.teaches: Her grief, laid on the son as a charge, is answered by the victory, so the battle closes the mother's wrong and not only the father's loss of the throne.

links.note: At 2308 Civakan is likened to the white moon seized by a serpent; at 2324 he is the young sun that splits the serpent's mouth after many days.
links.teaches: The eclipse image moves from moon in the serpent's grip in the thick of the fight to sun breaking free after the king's death, so the hero's figure grows brighter as the usurpation ends.

links.note: Kattiyangaran promised to guard the earth so it would brim with gold once the king had gone to heaven; at the end the Earth goddess, bathed in his allies' blood, is taken by Civakan.
links.teaches: The usurper's claim to be the earth's guardian is reversed by the closing marriage of earth and rightful heir, which shows the ilampakam's title answering his first speech of seizure.

source_issues: Nine stanzas (2308, 2309, 2311, 2316, 2318, 2323, 2324, 2325, 2326) were printed in eight half-lines and joined into four by the build.
2304 line 2 சோந்து and 2306 line 1 சோவபோல் appear to have lost an r (சோர்ந்து, சோர்வபோல்); 2306 and 2309 line 4 தோமிசை likewise for தேர்மிசை.
2309 line 4 ends இஞ்சினார், not a word as printed (perhaps துஞ்சினார்); line 3 நெஞ்சம looks truncated.
2313 line 2 செறித்திட்டு டஞ்சி has a doubled syllable.
2315 line 4 சந்து மாலியும் is obscure as divided.
2322 line 3 வெகுவத்துவர் is obscure as divided.
2323 line 4 விட்டமு தவன்கண் ஆர்வம் can be divided more than one way, changing whether the Earth puts away grief or gives her love.
